content: Ampicillin is an oral antibiotic approved by the FDA for treating various infections, including respiratory tract infections, bacterial infections, septicemia, endocarditis, urinary tract infections, and gastrointestinal infections. Common adverse reactions include anemia, thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopenic purpura, eosinophilia, leukopenia, agranulocytosis, hypersensitivity reactions, glossitis, and stomatitis. Adult Indications and Dosage: Ampicillin capsules are indicated for infections caused by susceptible strains of specific organisms. Genitourinary tract infections (including gonorrhea): Effective against E. coli, P. mirabilis, enterococci, Shigella, S. typhosa, other Salmonella species, and non-penicillinase-producing N. gonorrhoeae. Respiratory tract infections: Effective against non-penicillinase-producing H. influenzae, staphylococci, and streptococci, including Streptococcus pneumoniae. Gastrointestinal tract infections: Effective against Shigella, S. typhosa, other Salmonella species, E. coli, P. mirabilis, and enterococci. Meningitis: Effective against N. meningitidis. To prevent the development of drug-resistant bacteria, ampicillin should only be used for infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. Culture and susceptibility data should guide therapy whenever available. In the absence of such data, local epidemiology and susceptibility patterns may inform empiric therapy. Adults and children over 20 kg: For genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections (excluding gonorrhea), the usual dose is 500 mg four times daily (qid) in equally spaced doses. Severe or chronic infections may require higher doses. For gonorrhea, 5 grams of ampicillin administered simultaneously with 1 gram of probenecid is recommended. Follow-up cultures should be obtained 7 to 14 days after therapy. For respiratory tract infections, the usual dose is 250 mg qid in equally spaced doses. Children weighing 20 kg or less: For genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections, the usual dose is 100 mg/kg/day in four equally divided doses. For respiratory infections, the usual dose is 50 mg/kg/day in three to four equally divided doses. Pediatric doses should not exceed adult doses. Ampicillin should be administered at least 30 minutes before or 2 hours after meals for optimal absorption. Therapy should continue for at least 48 to 72 hours after symptoms resolve or bacterial eradication is confirmed. For infections caused by hemolytic streptococci, a minimum of 10 days of treatment is recommended to prevent rheumatic fever or glomerulonephritis. Chronic infections may require prolonged therapy and frequent monitoring. Contraindications: Ampicillin is contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity to penicillins or infections caused by penicillinase-producing organisms. Warnings: Serious and occasionally fatal hypersensitivity (anaphylactoid) reactions have been reported in patients receiving penicillin therapy. These reactions are more common in individuals with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity or multiple allergen sensitivities. Anaphylaxis requires immediate emergency treatment with epinephrine, oxygen, intravenous steroids, and airway management as needed. Pseudomembranous colitis has been reported with nearly all antibacterial agents, including ampicillin. It is important to consider this diagnosis in patients presenting with diarrhea following antibiotic administration. Adverse Reactions: Gastrointestinal: Glossitis, stomatitis, nausea, vomiting, enterocolitis, pseudomembranous colitis, and diarrhea. Hypersensitivity: Maculopapular rash, pruritus, urticaria, erythema multiforme, exfoliative dermatitis, and anaphylaxis. Liver: Moderate elevation in serum glutamic oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT). Hemic and lymphatic systems: Anemia, thrombocytopenia, thrombocytopenic purpura, eosinophilia, leukopenia, and agranulocytosis. Other reported reactions include laryngeal stridor, high fever, and sore mouth or tongue. Drug Interactions: Allopurinol: May increase the likelihood of skin rash, particularly in hyperuricemic patients. Bacteriostatic antibiotics (e.g., chloramphenicol, erythromycin, sulfonamides, tetracyclines): May interfere with the bactericidal effect of penicillins. Oral contraceptives: May be less effective, with increased breakthrough bleeding. Probenecid: May decrease renal tubular secretion of ampicillin, leading to increased blood levels and potential toxicity. Use in Specific Populations: Pregnancy: Classified as Category B by the FDA. Animal studies have shown no evidence of harm to the fetus, but adequate studies in pregnant women are lacking. Use during pregnancy only if clearly needed. Nursing mothers: Ampicillin is excreted in breast milk and may sensitize infants. A decision should be made to discontinue nursing or the drug, considering its importance to the mother. Pediatric use: Neonates and young infants with immature renal function may experience delayed excretion of penicillins. Dosage should be limited to the lowest effective amount. Geriatric use: No specific FDA guidance is available. Renal and hepatic impairment: No specific FDA guidance is available. Administration and Monitoring: Ampicillin should be administered orally. Monitoring information is limited in the drug label. Overdosage: In case of overdose, discontinue the medication, treat symptomatically, and provide supportive measures as needed. Ampicillin can be removed by hemodialysis but not by peritoneal dialysis. Pharmacology: Ampicillin is bactericidal at low concentrations and effective against a range of gram-positive and gram-negative organisms. It is stable in gastric acid and well-absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract. It diffuses into most body tissues and fluids but penetrates the cerebrospinal fluid only with meningeal inflammation. Ampicillin is largely excreted unchanged in the urine, and its excretion can be delayed by probenecid. Microbiology: Ampicillin is effective against various gram-positive and gram-negative organisms but is inactivated by penicillinase. It is ineffective against penicillinase-producing organisms, rickettsia, mycoplasma, and certain viruses. Storage: Store at 20°-25°C (68°-77°F). Patient Counseling: Limited information is available regarding patient counseling for oral ampicillin. Alcohol Interaction: The interaction between alcohol and ampicillin has not been established. Consult your doctor regarding the effects of alcohol with this medication. Brand Name: Ampicillin®
